newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK MP alleges leaks on Go-Ahead bid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK MP alleges leaks on Go-Ahead bid.

text.p: A British parliamentarian alleged on Wednesday that directors of a bus operator involved in bidding for a railways franchise might have leaked privileged information for use in illegal share dealing.

Labour MP Dale Campbell-Savours tabled a motion in the House of Commons that said directors of the Go-Ahead Group Plc leaked "price-sensitive, confidential and privileged information" concerning a proposed bid for the North East regional railways franchise to share speculators.
The insider-dealing allegation, which is protected from libel suits by parliamentary privilege, was immediately denied by Go-Ahead managing director Martin Ballinger.
"It's rubbish, absolute rubbish. I can't think of a more rude word to describe it than that," Ballinger told Reuters.
"Our share price rocketed up with the sector--it had nothing to do with the North East Railways bid," he added.

"Privileged access to information in the accounts of Regional Railways North East was used to convince those prepared to speculate that Go-Ahead were more likely than other bidders to take over the network," Savours said in the motion.
He called on government ministers to make a full statement to parliament on "which Go Ahead directors...were able to leak price-sensitive information for use in share speculation."

Go-Ahead shares have jumped more than 40 percent since a consortium of Go-Ahead, a North East railways management team and French group Via-GTI, was shortlisted by the government as a potential bidder for the franchise, which services major cities including Newcastle, York and Sheffield.
By early afternoon Go-Ahead shares were unchanged on the day at 488-1/2 pence.

Savours said in the motion that the London Stock Exchange was studying contacts between a group of British Rail managers and senior representatives of Go-Ahead as part of an investigation into possible illegal share dealing.
He alleged that the special knowledge about the franchise, held by "a group of British rail managers" was used in Go-Ahead's original bid in contravention of the government's own franchising rules.
The London Stock Exchange declined to confirm or deny an investigation was taking place. "I can say, however, that we always look at any unusual price movement in our shares," a spokesperson said.

Go-Ahead noted that in the bidding process it put in an "indicative" bid based on information which had more up-to-date accounts details because it had existing British Rail managers within its bid team.

But the company, which last September won the Thames Trains service from London to Oxford, said the franchise regulator Opraf had adjusted Go-Ahead's bid to bring the accounts information in line with other bidders.
"The final bids were all on basis of information available to all parties. There is no way we are in possession of price-sensitive information," Ballinger said.

The winner of the North East franchise is expected to be announced next week. To date, 18 of Britain's 25 railway networks have been privatised. The British government hopes to sell off the remaining seven franchises before a general election, which must take place by May 22.
The Opposition Labour Party, which currently holds a 20 percent lead in opinion polls, has been against the sell-off.
